extracted.intended_audience: federal jury and patent litigation practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions and legal standards for evaluating patent validity, equitable defenses, and damages in a patent infringement trial. Covers novelty, prior art, obviousness, inventorship, equitable defenses (inequitable conduct, laches, estoppel, prosecution laches, unclean hands), and damages (lost profits/reasonable royalty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty / Not new
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention is not new if the invention was made by someone else in the United States before the invention was made by [patent holder] and the other person did not abandon, suppress, or conceal the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an interference proceeding has been declared, additional instructions apply. Authorities cited include 35 U.S.C. § 102(a)-(g) and numerous Federal Circuit cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior Art — what counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art may include (1) items publicly known/used/on sale/made available before the filing date; (2) publications made available before the filing date; and (3) patents and published patent applications naming another inventor filed before the filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, prior art does not include an item/publication that is the inventor’s own work, describes the inventor’s own work, or was obtained directly/indirectly from the inventor unless it was made public more than one year before filing. Similarly, a patent/application that discloses the inventor’s work or was obtained from/owned by the same person may be excluded. Authorities: 35 U.S.C. § 102(a)(1)-(2), §102(b)(1)-(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation (anticipating prior art)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a claim to be invalid for lack of novelty (anticipation), the alleged infringer must show by clear and convincing evidence that all claim requirements were present in a single previous device, method, printed publication or patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The prior art reference need not use the same words as the claim, but must disclose all claim limitations, either expressly or inherently/impliedly to a person of ordinary skill in the art, so that that person could make and use the claimed invention from that one reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness — general standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed invention is unpatentable if it would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the field at the time the invention was made or before the effective filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alleged infringer must show invalidity by clear and convincing evidence. In assessing obviousness, consider (1) level of ordinary skill, (2) scope and content of prior art, and (3) differences between the prior art and the claimed invention. Do not use hindsight; evaluate claim-by-claim. The analysis is flexible and may consider whether a person would be prompted to combine known elements and whether prior art teaches/suggests/teaches away from combining them. A reasonable expectation of success is required for a finding of obviousness; 'obvious to try' is insufficient in unpredictable technologies. Authorities: 35 U.S.C. § 103; Graham v. John Deere; KSR v. Teleflex, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness — factors suggesting a reason to combine
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors to consider whether a person of ordinary skill would combine prior art elements include: (1) predictable result from using prior art elements according to known functions; (2) providing an obvious solution to a known problem; (3) prior art teaching/suggesting desirability of combining elements; (4) prior art teaching away from combining elements; (5) whether it would have been obvious to try combinations (finite predictable solutions/market pressure); and (6) whether change resulted from design incentives or market forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To find obviousness based on combination, the prior art must provide a reasonable expectation of success. 'Obvious to try' is not by itself sufficient in unpredictable arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary considerations (objective indicia) of nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective evidence that may bear on obviousness/nonobviousness includes: (a) commercial success due to merits of claimed invention; (b) satisfaction of a long-felt need; (c) others tried and failed; (d) independent, near-contemporaneous invention by others; (e) copying by others; (f) contemporaneous changes or market needs; (g) unexpected results; (h) praise from others in the field; (i) expressed surprise or disbelief by persons of ordinary skill; (j) licensing/transfer seeking of rights; (k) inventor proceeding contrary to accepted wisdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These objective factors should be considered as part of the obviousness analysis and can weigh against a finding of obviousness if present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of ordinary skill in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: In deciding the level of ordinary skill, consider evidence including: (1) education and experience of the inventor and others in the field; (2) types of problems encountered; (3) prior art solutions to those problems; (4) rapidity of innovation in the field; and (5) sophistication of the technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This factual determination informs obviousness and anticipation analyses. Authorities cited include Daiichi Sankyo v. Apotex and Ruiz v. A.B. Chance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and content of the prior art (analogous art)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scope and content of prior art includes at least prior art in the same field and also prior art from different fields that a person of ordinary skill would have considered when solving the invention’s problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If parties stipulate to prior art, use stipulated art; if disputed, fact-finders must determine the scope/content. Prior art not considered by the PTO may be weighed more heavily if materially different and more relevant than art considered during examination. Consider whether an inventor would have looked to that art to solve the problem (analogy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventorship requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent is invalid if it does not name all and only the actual inventors. To be an inventor one must make a significant contribution to the conception of at least one claim, measured against the scope of the full invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely explaining well-known concepts or carrying out instructions (experimentation) does not make one an inventor. Co-inventors need not contribute equally or to every claim and may be joint inventors without physically working together, but must have some open line of communication during or around the inventive effort. Authorities: 35 U.S.C. §§ 102, 256 and various Federal Circuit cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inequitable conduct — duty and elements
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant has a duty of candor and good faith to the PTO. Inequitable conduct occurs when a person involved in prosecution withholds material information or submits materially false information with intent to deceive the Examiner, rendering any resulting patent unenforceable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burden: alleged infringer must prove by clear and convincing evidence both materiality and intent to deceive. Materiality: information is material if the PTO would not have allowed the claim had it been aware; a false statement is material if it convinces the PTO to allow a claim it would not have otherwise. Affirmative egregious misconduct (e.g., filing an unmistakably false affidavit) is material. Intent: must be shown by direct evidence or inferred only if it is the single most reasonable inference; negligence, oversight, or gross negligence is insufficient. Materiality and intent are separate issues; both must be proven by clear and convincing evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laches (delay-based equitable defense)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laches is asserted when the patent holder delayed filing suit for an unreasonably long and inexcusable time and the alleged infringer was or will be materially prejudiced as a result. Alleged infringer must prove delay and prejudice by a preponderance of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No minimum delay required; a six-year delay gives rise to a rebuttable presumption of unreasonableness and prejudice shifting burden to patent holder to justify delay. Justifying facts can include involvement in other litigation, negotiations, poverty/illness, wartime, ownership disputes, or minimal infringing activity. Prejudice may be evidentiary (lost records, witnesses, memories) or economic (changed economic position such that losses beyond paying for infringement occurred). Ultimately laches is a fairness inquiry and may be declined even if elements are shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: Equitable estoppel bars the patent holder from relief where (1) the patent holder made a misleading communication about noninfringement or not suing, (2) the alleged infringer relied on that communication, and (3) the alleged infringer will be materially harmed if the patent holder is allowed to assert an inconsistent claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communications may be written, spoken, conduct, silence, or combinations. Material harm can be evidentiary or economic. The alleged infringer must prove each element by a preponderance of the evidence, but even if proven the court may decline estoppel if fairness dictates otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution laches
rubrics_metrics.description: Prosecution laches bars enforcement where there was an unreasonably long delay in securing patent claims (from original application to asserted patent application) and allowing enforcement would prejudice the infringer, another party, or the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the facts/circumstances during the delay period; consider investment by others in products now covered by the patent, whether others may be subject to infringement, whether the public’s free practice was unduly postponed, and whether delay was intentional/deliberate and known to others that applications were pending. Authorities include cases finding forfeiture after very long prosecution delays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unclean hands (equitable defense)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unclean hands may bar enforcement where the patent owner acted inequitably, unfairly, or deceitfully toward the infringer or the Court in a way that has immediate and necessary relation to the relief sought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a fact-specific balancing of all circumstances; alleged infringer bears the preponderance standard. Authorities include Keystone Driller and other cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages — general principles
rubrics_metrics.description: If infringement of a valid claim is found, damages must adequately compensate the patent holder (not punish) and put the patent holder in approximately the position it would have been absent infringement. Patent holder bears the burden to establish damages by a preponderance of the evidence and must prove them with reasonable certainty (not mere speculation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different types of damages include lost profits and reasonable royalties. Damages must be tied to the intrinsic value of the patented feature (no recovery for remote or speculative consequences). Where damages cannot be ascertained precisely, doubts are resolved against the alleged infringer if the inability is due to the infringer’s own poor recordkeeping. If the patent holder committed to RAND licensing, damages must be consistent with RAND obligations. Authorities: 35 U.S.C. § 284 and numerous Federal Circuit cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty (definition and floor)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reasonable royalty is the monetary amount the patent holder and alleged infringer would have agreed upon as a fee for use of the invention at a time before infringement began.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent holder is entitled to recover at least a reasonable royalty for each infringing sale. Ensure the royalty sought is no more or less than the value of the patented invention and is consistent with RAND obligations if applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost profits — the 'but for' (Panduit) test and elements
rubrics_metrics.description: To recover lost profits, the patent holder must show a causal relationship between infringement and lost profit — i.e., that but for the infringement there is a reasonable probability the patent holder would have earned higher profits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The patent holder must establish each of the following: (1) demand for the patented product/method/product produced by method; (2) absence of acceptable, noninfringing substitutes, or if substitutes existed, the patent holder’s market share that it would have made despite their availability; (3) manufacturing and marketing capacity to make the sales for which lost profits are sought; and (4) the amount of profit the patent holder would have made but for the infringement. Authorities: 35 U.S.C. § 284; Panduit and related cases are cited.
